title: The Agile Onion: five layers
blurb: Name the five layers of the Agile Onion, say what each contains, and explain why change at the core lasts longest.
question: In the Agile Onion, which layer is made up of specific techniques such as prioritization and activities such as workshops?

teach.body: PRINCE2 Agile uses the Agile Onion to show that agility has layers. The syllabus lists five: processes, practices, principles, values and mindset. That is a list, not a ranking by visibility. Processes and practices are what you can see a team using, and the book calls practices the most visible part of agile adoption. Principles, values and mindset are what the team believes and how it thinks, with the mindset as the innermost core. In plain English: you can copy a team's meetings in a day, but not its way of thinking.

teach.h: From the outer layers to the core
teach.topLabel: Core: the mindset drives lasting change
teach.bottomLabel: Outer: practices are the most visible

What it is
Book's key point
rows: Give structure; alone do not guarantee agility
Most visible; only scratch the surface

teach.h: Processes and practices: the outer layers
teach.body: Processes are the formal processes of agile frameworks. They guide teams on when to deliver value and how to manage work, but the book says they do not guarantee agility unless deeper principles and values leave room for change and innovation. Practices are specific techniques, such as prioritization, and activities, such as events and workshops. They are the most visible part of agile adoption, yet they only scratch the surface: a team that stops here may look agile without the depth needed for long-term success.

teach.h: Principles and values: the 'why' and the foundation
teach.body: Principles are the core guidelines that steer agile behaviour. They derive from the Agile Manifesto, for example welcoming changing requirements even late in development. Teams that internalize them understand why they use their practices and processes. Values are defined by the Agile Manifesto and are the foundation of agile that encompasses all else. They move the focus from rigid processes to people, collaboration and user value.

At the centre is the mindset: a way of thinking and approaching work that fosters adaptability and encourages continual learning, improvement and flexibility. Change here lasts longest because it shapes every layer around it. When pressure rises, a team with only new practices tends to slip back to old habits; a team whose values and mindset have shifted keeps adapting, and will even redesign its practices to suit.

Tarrant Mutual's claims team adopted stand-ups, a Kanban board and MoSCoW prioritization in one month. When a regulator deadline loomed, it abandoned them and went back to long approval chains. Agile coach Daniel Osei restarted with the inner layers: workshops on the Manifesto's values, why each principle mattered, and what the team believed about change. Six months later, under a second deadline, the team adapted its board instead of abandoning it.

teach.text: Do not confuse values and principles. Values are the foundation that encompasses all else (from the Manifesto's four values). Principles are the guidelines derived from the Manifesto, such as welcoming late changes, that explain the 'why'. And practices, not values, are the most visible layer.

items: Five layers: processes, practices, principles, values, mindset.
Processes give structure but do not guarantee agility on their own.
Practices (techniques and activities) are the most visible but only scratch the surface.
Principles come from the Manifesto and explain the 'why'; values are the foundation that encompasses all else.
Mindset is the way of thinking at the core; change there lasts longest.

summary: You can now name the five Agile Onion layers (processes, practices, principles, values, mindset) and say what each contains. You can also explain why change at the inner layers lasts longer than adopting visible practices and processes.

A.q: Which of these is one of the five layers of the Agile Onion?
A.why: The five layers are processes, practices, principles, values and mindset (2.6.1).

whyNot.0: Roles belong to the organization practice, not the Agile Onion.
whyNot.1: Artifacts such as the release map are PRINCE2 Agile products, not an Onion layer.
whyNot.3: Tolerances belong to managing by exception, not the Agile Onion.

A.q: Which Agile Onion layer is made up of specific techniques, such as prioritization, and activities, such as events and workshops?
A.why: Practices are the specific techniques and activities used in agile frameworks (2.6.1).

whyNot.1: Principles are the core guidelines that steer behaviour, not techniques and events.
whyNot.2: Processes are the formal processes of frameworks that give structure.
whyNot.3: Values are the foundation defined by the Manifesto, not techniques.

A.q: Which Agile Onion layer is defined by the Agile Manifesto and described as the foundation of agile that encompasses all else?
A.why: Values are defined by the Agile Manifesto and are the foundation of agile that encompasses all else (2.6.1).

whyNot.0: Principles derive from the Manifesto too, but they are the guidelines that explain the 'why'.
whyNot.1: Practices are techniques and activities, the most visible layer.
whyNot.2: Mindset is the way of thinking; the book calls values the foundation that encompasses all else.

B.q: Which Agile Onion layer derives from the Agile Manifesto and, once internalized, helps a team understand the 'why' behind its practices?
B.why: Principles are the core guidelines derived from the Manifesto; teams that internalize them understand the 'why' behind practices and processes (2.6.1).

whyNot.0: Processes give structure but need deeper principles and values to support them.
whyNot.2: Practices are what teams do; principles explain why they do it.
whyNot.3: Values are the foundation that encompasses all else, not the guidelines explaining the 'why'.

B.q: A team adopts a framework's formal processes for deciding when to deliver value. What does PRINCE2 Agile say about this layer?
options: It is the foundation that encompasses all else
It gives structure but does not guarantee agility
It is the way of thinking that drives the rest
It explains the 'why' behind the techniques
B.why: Processes give structure, guiding when to deliver value and how to manage work, but alone they do not guarantee agility (2.6.1).

B.q: Identify the missing word in the following sentence. In the Agile Onion, the [?] is a way of thinking and approaching work that fosters adaptability.
B.why: The mindset is the way of thinking and approaching work that fosters adaptability and continual learning (2.6.1).

whyNot.0: Practices are techniques and activities, not a way of thinking.
whyNot.1: Principles are guidelines that steer behaviour, derived from the Manifesto.
whyNot.2: Processes are formal framework processes that give structure.

C.q:
Which two statements about the Agile Onion are correct?
1. Principles derive from the Agile Manifesto.
2. Practices are the deepest layer of the onion.
3. Processes are enough to guarantee agility.
4. Values are the foundation that encompasses all else.
C.why: Principles derive from the Manifesto (1) and values are the foundation that encompasses all else (4) (2.6.1).

whyNot.0: Statement 2 is wrong: practices are the most visible layer, not the deepest.
whyNot.1: Both are wrong: practices are visible, and processes alone do not guarantee agility.
whyNot.2: Statement 3 is wrong: processes need deeper principles and values to support them.

C.q: At Morwen Builders, a site team quickly adopted stand-ups, retrospectives and MoSCoW, and looked agile. Under deadline pressure it dropped them all. Which layer had the team reached, and what does PRINCE2 Agile say about it?
options: Values, which are the most visible part of adoption
Mindset, which lasts only while practices continue
Practices, which only scratch the surface of agility
Principles, which give structure without the 'why'
C.why: Stand-ups, retrospectives and MoSCoW are practices. They are the most visible part of adoption but only scratch the surface; teams stopping there lack the depth for long-term success (2.6.1).

whyNot.0: Values are an inner layer; the most visible layer is practices.
whyNot.1: The mindset is the inner core that drives the rest; the team never reached it.
whyNot.3: Principles explain the 'why'; structure is what processes provide.

C.q: A transformation lead wants agile ways of working that survive pressure. Where should the effort focus, and why?
options: On processes, because structure creates agility
On values and mindset, because they drive lasting change
On practices, because they are the most visible layer
On terminology, because shared words shape behaviour
C.why: Values are the foundation that encompasses all else and the mindset is the way of thinking at the core; without them, practices and processes lack the depth for long-term success (2.6.1).

whyNot.0: Processes alone do not guarantee agility; they need deeper principles and values.
whyNot.2: Practices are visible but only scratch the surface of agility.
whyNot.3: Terminology is part of doing agile and is not an Onion layer.

reteach.title: The tree and its roots
reteach.question: Why does PRINCE2 Agile draw agility as layers?

blocks.body: Think of a tree. Leaves and branches (practices and processes) are what people notice and photograph. The trunk (principles) carries the reasons. The roots (values) hold everything up, and the soil they grow in (mindset) decides whether the tree thrives. Strip the leaves and a healthy tree grows them back; glue leaves onto a dead branch and they fall at the first storm.

blocks.text: The most visible layer is practices, not values. Values are the foundation; principles explain the 'why'.

explain.body: Processes, practices, principles, values and mindset (2.6.1).

explain.caption: Outer layers at the base (practices most visible), mindset at the core.

test.q: Which list gives the five layers of the Agile Onion?
test.why: The five layers are processes, practices, principles, values and mindset (2.6.1).

whyNot.0: Roles, artifacts and events are not Onion layers.
whyNot.2: Themes and behaviours are not Onion layers; 'themes' is an older PRINCE2 term.
whyNot.3: Tools, techniques and tolerances are not Onion layers.

explain.body: Processes give structure but do not guarantee agility. Practices are techniques and activities; the most visible layer, they only scratch the surface (2.6.1).

test.q: Which Agile Onion layer does PRINCE2 Agile describe as the most visible part of agile adoption?
test.why: Practices are the most visible aspects of agile adoption but only scratch the surface of true agility (2.6.1).

whyNot.0: Values are the foundation, an inner layer.
whyNot.1: Principles explain the 'why' and sit beneath the practices.
whyNot.2: Mindset is the way of thinking at the core.

explain.body: Principles derive from the Manifesto and explain the 'why'. Values are defined by the Manifesto and are the foundation that encompasses all else, focusing on people, collaboration and user value (2.6.1).

test.q: 'Welcome changing requirements, even late in development' is an example from which Agile Onion layer?
test.why: Principles derive from the Agile Manifesto; welcoming changing requirements is one of them (2.6.1).

whyNot.1: Practices are techniques and activities such as prioritization and workshops.
whyNot.3: Mindset is the way of thinking, not a stated guideline.

explain.body: Teams that adopt only practices may look agile but lack the depth for long-term success. The mindset at the core shapes everything around it (2.6.1).

test.q: According to PRINCE2 Agile, what may happen to a team that focuses only on practices?
options: It reaches the mindset more quickly
It may look agile but lack depth
It gains a lasting cultural shift
It replaces the need for principles
test.why: Teams focusing only on practices may appear agile but lack the depth of mindset needed for long-term success (2.6.1).

whyNot.0: Practices only scratch the surface; they do not reach the mindset.
whyNot.2: A lasting cultural shift comes from being agile, not practices alone.
whyNot.3: Practices need principles to explain why they are used.
